title: Miscellanies in Verse and Prose
description: John Dennis's first collected volume, a miscellany of occasional verse, translations and short critical and philosophical papers assembled at the close of the stage controversy and the battle of the books. It carries his early essay of a critical personality: ambitious native verse, a partisan defence of the new English prosody, and a habit of turning quarrels into theory. The volume antedates the nominal scope of this installment, but is entered here because Dennis's critical importance belongs wholly to the Augustan age that followed.
plot_or_argument: The volume mixes modes without pretending a single argument: poems of mourning, praise and compliment sit beside prose pieces on the drama, on learning and on the manners of the time, and all are informed by two convictions that Dennis spent the next forty years elaborating. These are, first, that modern poetry in the living languages has genuinely advanced upon the ancient model, and secondly, that its advance is purchased at a moral cost which the critic, not the player, must police. The miscellany's pose is therefore that of the corrective censor who is also a practising poet.
narrative_structure: A printed miscellany of independent pieces, sequenced by the editor's sense of proportion rather than by argument, with verse and prose interleaved and each item carrying its own dedication or occasion.
literary_form: collected miscellany of verse and critical prose
meter_and_prosody: Occasional verse chiefly in the heroic couplet and in the looser stanzaic forms of the commendatory and elegiac tradition; prose of the heightened, syntactically straining Augustan critical style Dennis made his own.
historical_context: Published in the immediate aftermath of the 1690s quarrel over the stage and of the ancient-modern dispute, when a hard-up writer could turn a miscellany into a manifesto and a subscription pitch; Dennis's later career as a professed critic, dependent on patrons and on the book trade, begins here.
literary_significance: It marks the appearance in English letters of the professional critic as a public character with a theory of his own, and it gathers the first drafts of the ideas of enthusiasm, magnificence and native poetical advancement that the great treatises of 1701 and 1704 would systematise.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the volume carries Dennis's name. The dating of individual pieces within it is not fixed here.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1693; the volume is dated earlier than the 1700-89 field of this installment and is entered as the foundation of a critically Augustan career. No printer or format is asserted beyond the 1693 imprint on the title page.

title: The Advancement and Reformation of Modern Poetry
description: Dennis's first major critical treatise, arguing that modern poetry in the European vernaculars has genuinely advanced upon the ancients, chiefly by the invention of rhyme and by the access a Christian and gallant age gives to terrors and refinements of passion unknown to antiquity. Its second half turns from advancement to reformation, urging that the same gifts have been wasted by a corrupt stage and by a mercenary book trade. The book is the founding document of Dennis's lifelong case for enthusiasm as the life-blood of great writing.
plot_or_argument: Dennis maintains that the rules of the ancients are rules of nature, and that where modern practice satisfies nature more fully than ancient practice it deserves the preference; rhyme is defended not as a barbaric licence but as an artifice that supplies the sound and measure that English verse needs. The greater heights, however, are reached only by poetic enthusiasm, a kind of elevated transport proper to poetry and quite distinct from the reasoning craft of criticism. Against this standard the present age is then arraigned: the stage has debased its patrons' morals, the dunces have debased its praise, and the reform of poetry must therefore be at once technical and moral.
narrative_structure: A continuous argumentative treatise in two movements, advancement and reformation, each built from numbered heads and supported by example from the modern poets, with a polemical conclusion addressed to the present state of the drama and of letters.
meter_and_prosody: Prose; the style is deliberately emphatical, with long periodic structures, triple weight, and a syntax that strains toward the sublime it theorises.
historical_context: Issued in the season still dominated by the stage-morality quarrel opened by Collier in 1698 and by the party and denominational warfare of the last years of William's reign; Dennis wrote as an obscure dependant of patrons and of the theatre he simultaneously defended and attacked.
literary_significance: It put the defence of rhyme and the theory of poetical enthusiasm on the English agenda a generation before the sublime became common property, and supplied the vocabulary in which Addison, Hughes, Akenside and later the French critics of the genie enthousiaste would conduct their debates.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; Dennis's authorship is documented by his own subsequent collection of his critical works.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1701 and subsequently reissued within Dennis's collected critical works; the standard modern reading text is that of the scholarly edition of his prose.

title: The Grounds of Criticism in Poetry
description: Dennis's systematic companion to the treatise of 1701, which sets out the foundations of a critical art: poetry is an imitative and designing craft whose ends are to instruct and delight, whose means are the passions, and whose highest achievements depend upon enthusiasm, both ordinary and poetical. The argument grounds the rules in nature and in the reason of things, and then argues from the same premises that the religion of a modern nation is a necessary foundation of its poetry. It is the most rigorous of Dennis's attempts to hold neoclassical rule and Augustan sublimity in one system.
plot_or_argument: Dennis first disposes of the sceptical objection that criticism is a vain art, insisting that as surely as the rules of music produce harmony the rules of poetry, learned from nature and from the ancients, produce pleasure; he then distinguishes the passions that a poet must know from the craft that copies them, and derives from this the doctrine that great poetry requires an enthusiastick elevation which no mere rule-making can supply. He next argues that a religion of terrors and of grandeur such as Christianity provides gives the modern poet materials the pagan epics never possessed, while the machinery of a revealed faith is at once more awful and more instructive than the personifications of the heathens. Finally he tests the moderns against the ancients in the several genres, and finds that the critic's office is to reconcile the love of the ancients with the claims of a more knowing age.
narrative_structure: A treatise advancing in numbered sections and argumentative heads from first principles to the doctrine of enthusiasm, then to religion as the foundation of modern poetry, then to an evaluation of the modern genres, with a closing defence of the critical enterprise itself.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, in the emphatical and heavily coordinated style Dennis associated with grandeur, with long periods, balanced clauses and repeated key terms.
historical_context: Published in the last years of the reign of Queen Anne's precedent period of the Whig war and the expedition to the continent, when Dennis, an ardent Williamite, was writing against the Tory revival in letters; it was reprinted after his death, in the age of the Scottish enquiry into taste, because it was one of the few native treatises on enthusiasm available to eighteenth-century readers.
literary_significance: It is the chief English link between Renaissance poetics of the rules and the eighteenth-century psychology of enthusiasm, the sublime and genius, and much of what Addison, Hughes, the Blairs and the French theorists said on those subjects was worked out first in these pages.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1704 and afterwards collected with Dennis's other critical treatises; the title page of the first issue carries the date 1704.

title: Appius and Virginia
description: Dennis's blank-verse Roman tragedy, drawn from the decemviral history of Livy, in which the lust of the mighty magistrate for a plebeian maid and the father's pious murder of her become a study of corrupt power, chastity and republican fury. Severe in its moral register and unstinted in its invective against the decemvirs, it is the dramatic illustration of the theories of enthusiasm and of the terrors of virtue set out in the treatises of 1701 and 1704. Its failure at the playhouse and the quarrel over its re-use by other authors made it also the most famous case in the century of the professional writer's grievance.
plot_or_argument: Appius, one of the decemvirs, designs to get Virginia, the betrothed of Icilius, by a judicial fiction of sale, and uses his authority to defeat her advocates in the forum; Virginius, her father, rather than yield her to the tyrant's power, kills her in the street with a sentence that at once frees and destroys her; the outraged commons secede, the decemviral yoke is attacked, and Appius, stripped of office and abandoned by his patrons, dies in captivity. The play thus moves from the corruption of law into tyranny, to private catastrophe, and then to the restoration of public liberty.
narrative_structure: Regular five-act tragedy in the neoclassical manner, with a public forum action, a central recognition and killing, and an offstage political resolution; the catastrophe is reported rather than represented, and the political action closes the design.
principal_characters: Appius Claudius; Virginia; Virginius; Icilius; the seceding commons of Rome
literary_form: tragedy in five acts, written for the stage
meter_and_prosody: Unrhymed iambic pentameter, declamatory and heavily sententious, with long impassioned periods and a deliberate accumulation of terror-words proper to Dennis's account of poetical enthusiasm.
historical_context: First acted in London in 1709, in a season when the theatre was contested ground for Whig and Tory interpretations of Roman liberty; it held the stage for only a very short run, and the later revival of its scenes in another company's play provoked Dennis's well-known public protest against the appropriation of his work.
literary_significance: Its severity and its political indignation made it a permanent exemplum of the neglected Augustan tragedian, and the anecdote attached to it entered the common lore of authorial property in dramatic texts; it also survives as the practical test case of a critical theory that demanded terror, enthusiasm and moral gravity in the same play.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; Dennis's ownership of the text is documented by his own publication and by the anecdote of the reclaimed scenes.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in London in 1709 concurrent with the first performances; the exact number of nights and the precise day of first performance are not asserted here, nor is the title of the revived play into which the company carried his scenes.

title: The School-Master
description: William Shenstone's earliest considerable poem, a pastoral eclogue in three parts which memorialises his old schoolmaster and turns the village school into an Arcadian scene. The poem honors the learned country usher, sketches his poverty and his patience, and asks what returns a nation makes to the men who form its youth. It is at once a tribute, a pastoral of letters, and a complaint about the treatment of the obscure teacher, and it announced the distinctive Shenstonian mixture of tenderness, rural observation and self-conscious antiquarianism.
plot_or_argument: In the first part the scene of the school is drawn in pastoral disguise, the master's patience and cares mustered, and the poet recalls the benefit he personally received; in the second the ageing master's distresses and his dependence upon a generous eye are set out with a melancholy directness; the third part resolves the poem into an address to the patron and to the Muses, asking that the man who taught others to live should not be left to die neglected. The design is thus tripartite in feeling as well as in form: recollection, complaint, and petition.
narrative_structure: A pastoral eclogue in three parts, framed by an invocation and a dedicatory address, moving from recalled schoolroom scene to present complaint to closing petition, with the shepherd-poet convention carrying the memoir.
principal_characters: the schoolmaster; the pupil-poet; the neighbouring rustics and pupils
literary_form: pastoral eclogue in three parts, with argument and annotations
meter_and_prosody: An uneven pastoral stanza of short iambic lines, in the deliberate archaisms and irregularities of the English eclogue tradition inherited from Spenser and from the seventeenth-century school of the shepheardes calendars; Shenstone's own notes on the stanza's antiquity accompany the poem.
historical_context: Published in 1742, when the country retired gentleman and the minor poet of the counties were a recognised figure in the literary geography outside London, and when the school-master was a stock of both charity sermon and satire; Shenstone printed and circulated his poems largely through friends and local presses rather than through the great London houses.
literary_significance: It gave the century one of its most reprinted poems of gratitude and educational piety, helped to fix the image of the poor country schoolmaster in British feeling, and stands with Shenstone's Leasowes writings as a document of the mid-century culture of retirement, sensibility and rural taste.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; Shenstone's authorship is documented by his own circulation of the poem and by the collected editions of his works.
bibliographical_notes: First published separately in 1742 in a privately sponsored impression; the poem was thereafter reprinted in the collected editions of Shenstone's works and in the standard school anthologies. The identity of the schoolmaster commemorated is not asserted here.

title: Written in the Eleventh Century
description: Shenstone's late meditative poem, which situates its speaker by conceit in the eleventh century and so makes the present a remote antiquity. The resulting double perspective - an early age contemplating its own ruins, and a modern reader discovering his own remoteness - is the poem's machinery, and it turns the graveyard meditation outward upon history. It is Shenstone's most purely philosophical verse and one of the neatly depressing classics of preromantic reflection.
plot_or_argument: The speaker, casting thought back into a millennium already gone, surveys what the vanished centuries had built and what time had spared, and finds that the proudest works of men stand in the same relation to the future as the ruins he contemplates to the past; the poem therefore proceeds by a chain of retrospection and anticipation, in which nations, foundations, learns and families alike are made to look forward to their own oblivion. It closes not in despair but in the tempered resignation proper to the moralised melancholy of the age, the reader being left to imagine his own century as the eleventh.
narrative_structure: A continuous meditative poem, moving by association through a sequence of historical retrospect and prospective fancy, without dramatic or argumentative division; the conceit of the dating is itself the organising principle.
principal_characters: the meditating antiquary-speaker; the vanished ages and their founders
meter_and_prosody: Unrhymed iambic pentameter of the mid-century reflective school, with a slow, suspended syntax, frequent apostrophe and a marked fondness for the balanced pair of past and future.
historical_context: Published in 1759, the year that also brought the first collected reputation of Young's meditations, the vogue of the graveyard, and the first great quarrel over the authenticity of ancient native poetry; Shenstone was then at the Leasowes, writing and planting, and the poem's temper of retired retrospect belongs to that scene.
literary_significance: It carries the graveyard meditation from the churchyard into historical time, anticipating the philosophy of ruin and of the distant century that would occupy the preromantic and romantic generations, and it long remained the standard anthology instance of Shenstone as a thinker rather than merely a poet of gardens.
bibliographical_notes: Published in 1759; the venue of first issue, and whether it appeared separately or within a miscellany of the year, is not asserted here, and the poem is normally read from the collected editions of Shenstone's works.
